intro.prologue: January 2009. You're a tech student with a gaming PC, a couple thousand dollars saved, and a part-time job that covers pizza and rent-free living at home. A program a stranger posted on a mailing list just started running on your machine — something about decentralized digital cash, signed by a name nobody can place. It isn't worth anything. There's no market for it, no exchange, no price. You leave it running anyway, because it costs you nothing but electricity your parents are already paying for, and because you're curious. Eight years from now, in a garage, this decision will still be the one that matters most.
tooltip.p0.difficulty: Difficulty is how hard the network makes the puzzle. It rises as more machines join — in the early years it barely moves; by 2013 it doubles some months.
tooltip.p0.solo_vs_pool: Solo mining means you keep everything you find, but you might find nothing for months. A pool pays you your fair share every week, minus a small fee. Solo is a good bet when almost nobody else is mining; it stops being one as the network grows.
tooltip.p0.custody: Coins on an exchange can be sold instantly, but they're the exchange's problem if it gets hacked or collapses. Coins in your own wallet are yours alone — until you lose the keys.
tooltip.p0.backup: A wallet backup costs you almost nothing and cuts your chance of losing everything to a dead hard drive by most of the way. Do it before you need it, not after.
tooltip.p0.preorders: Paying an ASIC vendor up front, before the hardware exists, can beat buying GPUs — if it ships close to on time. Most pre-orders in this era shipped late. Some never shipped at all.
tooltip.p0.hodl_sell: Each quarter, choose how much of what you mine to sell. In the early years there's barely a price to sell at; later, it's the difference between paying rent and betting on the future.
glossary.genesis_block: The very first block of a blockchain, mined before any transactions existed to reference. Bitcoin's genesis block was mined 3 Jan 2009.
glossary.difficulty: How hard the network makes the mining puzzle. It rises as more machines join, so each machine earns less over time.
glossary.halving: Every four years or so, the block reward is cut in half. Bitcoin's first halving (Nov 2012) cut it from 50 to 25 coins.
glossary.solo_mining: Mining alone: you keep the whole block reward if you find one, but the odds of finding one drop as the network grows.
glossary.pool: A group of miners who combine their hashing power and split the rewards, usually for a small fee, so payouts are steady instead of a lottery.
glossary.pps: Pay Per Share: a pool pays you a fixed amount for every valid share you submit, whether or not the pool actually finds a block. The pool takes on the risk; fees are usually higher.
glossary.pplns: Pay Per Last N Shares: when a pool finds a block, the reward is split among the most recent shares submitted. You take on more of the variance; fees are usually lower.
glossary.fpga: Field-Programmable Gate Array: a chip you can reprogram for a specific job. Briefly the most efficient way to mine bitcoin, between GPUs and dedicated ASICs.
glossary.asic: A chip built for exactly one job. Bitcoin ASICs vastly outperform GPUs at mining but can do nothing else.
glossary.pre_order: Paying for hardware before it's built. Cheaper than buying finished units, but you're gambling on the vendor actually delivering — and delivering before the difficulty rises out from under you.
glossary.hot_wallet: A wallet connected to the internet (on an exchange, or on a machine that's always online). Convenient, and a bigger target.
glossary.cold_storage: Keeping your private keys somewhere offline — a piece of paper, an unplugged drive. Safer from hacks, but yours alone to lose.
glossary.private_key: The secret number that proves you own a bitcoin address. Lose it, and the coins at that address are gone for good; no bank to call.
glossary.exchange: A site where you can trade coins for dollars (or other coins). Convenient for selling; a single point of failure if it's hacked or collapses.
news.2009Q4.0: A forum post proposes the first exchange rate for bitcoin: 1,309.03 coins to the dollar
news.2010Q2.0: A Florida programmer pays 10,000 coins for two pizzas
news.2010Q3.0: A small Japanese trading card site relaunches as a bitcoin exchange
news.2010Q3.1: A software bug briefly creates 184 billion coins before the network patches itself
news.2010Q4.0: The first pooled mining service opens; miners can now split rewards instead of gambling alone
news.2011Q1.0: Bitcoin reaches parity with the US dollar for the first time
news.2011Q2.0: Bitcoin touches $31 before a hacked exchange account crashes the price toward a cent
news.2011Q4.0: Bitcoin bottoms near $2, down more than 90% from June's high
news.2012Q4.0: The first halving cuts the block reward from 50 to 25 coins
news.2013Q1.0: The first purpose-built mining chips start taking pre-orders
news.2013Q2.0: A Cyprus banking crisis is credited with a bitcoin rally past $260
news.2013Q4.0: Federal agents shut down the Silk Road marketplace and seize tens of thousands of coins
news.2013Q4.1: Bitcoin crosses $1,000 for the first time
news.2013Q4.2: China bars its financial institutions from bitcoin business; the price drops hard
news.2014Q1.0: The exchange that dominates bitcoin trading halts withdrawals, then goes offline, then files for bankruptcy
news.2015Q3.0: A new blockchain, Ethereum, launches with its own coin and its own miners
news.2016Q3.0: A smart contract holding millions of the new coin is drained overnight
news.2016Q3.1: The second halving cuts bitcoin's block reward from 25 to 12.5 coins
news.2016Q3.2: A newer, more efficient mining machine goes on sale at a steep launch price
news.2016Q3.3: Another exchange loses roughly 120,000 coins to hackers
news.2016Q4.0: Eight years in, you're carrying everything you built into a real operation
